steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
In practice, data analytics for business planning and operations is usually organized as a pipeline, which is a sequential set of processes that turn collected raw data into business decisions to be implemented. To prescribe operational decisions, mathematical programming models (e.g., for production planning) usually sit in the downstream stages of the pipeline, and their inputs come from upstream processes, e.g., statistical models for product demand learned with machine learning methods. In this approach learning and optimization are done separately and one after the other. It is intuitive to implement, but it can be suboptimal, since the learning phase often does not take into account how its outputs are used as inputs in the downstream optimization phase.

In this paper we look at a prescriptive analytics pipeline whose goal is to prescribe a set of optimal decisions in a stochastic optimization problem, given high-dimensional input data. More specifically, there are two sequential phases: (1) a dimensionality reduction phase, which learns a low-dimensional representation of the probability distribution that generates the high-dimensional data; and (2) a stochastic optimization phase, which prescribes an optimal solution to a stochastic program where the parameter uncertainty is governed by this distribution. This kind of scenario has many practical applications. For example, an urban mobility platform may optimize the repositioning of its fleet using a probability distribution of travel demand that is learned from data. In these applications the raw origin-destination travel data can be high dimensional, but the variations in the underlying demand distribution are often governed by a low-dimensional structure with a smaller number of factors.

Our research objectives are the following. First, we look at the limitation of using standard dimensionality reduction methods (like principal component analysis, PCA) in this two-phase scenario. In particular, we show that standard PCA can fail to find the factors that are relevant to the downstream stochastic program. Second, since PCA has this shortcoming in aligning the two phases of the problem, we propose a prescriptive alternative which learns a low-dimensional representation of the data that minimizes the downstream suboptimality. We use distributionally-robust optimization techniques to show that the problem of minimizing a proxy (an upper bound) for how suboptimal the downstream stochastic program is can be formulated as a bi-convex problem. A local optimal solution to this problem can be found with an alternating algorithm that solves a semidefinite program in each iteration. Third, we use synthetic and real data to test how effective our approach is, on a joint production and inventory allocation problem for a supply chain network and on a vehicle repositioning problem for an urban mobility platform.

steps.text:
In practice, data analytics for business planning and operations is usually organized as a pipeline, which is a sequential set of processes that turn collected raw data into business decisions to be implemented. To prescribe operational decisions, mathematical programming models (e.g., for production planning) usually sit in the downstream stages of the pipeline, and their inputs come from upstream processes, e.g., statistical models for product demand learned with machine learning methods. In this approach learning and optimization are done separately and one after the other. It is intuitive to implement, but it can be suboptimal, since the learning phase often does not take into account how its outputs are used as inputs in the downstream optimization phase.

In this paper we look at a prescriptive analytics pipeline whose goal is to prescribe a set of optimal decisions in a stochastic optimization problem, given high-dimensional input data. More specifically, there are two sequential phases: (1) a dimensionality reduction phase, which learns a low-dimensional representation of the probability distribution that generates the high-dimensional data; and (2) a stochastic optimization phase, which prescribes an optimal solution to a stochastic program where the parameter uncertainty is governed by this distribution. This kind of scenario has many practical applications. For example, an urban mobility platform may optimize the repositioning of its fleet using a probability distribution of travel demand that is learned from data. In these applications the raw origin-destination travel data can be high dimensional, but the variations in the underlying demand distribution are often governed by a low-dimensional structure with a smaller number of factors.

Our research objectives are the following. First, we look at the limitation of using standard dimensionality reduction methods (like principal component analysis, PCA) in this two-phase scenario. In particular, we show that standard PCA can fail to find the factors that are relevant to the downstream stochastic program. Second, since PCA has this shortcoming in aligning the two phases of the problem, we propose a prescriptive alternative which learns a low-dimensional representation of the data that minimizes the downstream suboptimality. We use distributionally-robust optimization techniques to show that the problem of minimizing a proxy (an upper bound) for how suboptimal the downstream stochastic program is can be formulated as a bi-convex problem. A local optimal solution to this problem can be found with an alternating algorithm that solves a semidefinite program in each iteration. Third, we use synthetic and real data to test how effective our approach is, on a joint production and inventory allocation problem for a supply chain network and on a vehicle repositioning problem for an urban mobility platform.

## 1.1 Related Literature

Our work is related to the literature on mathematical programming and on machine learning.

Interface of Machine Learning and Optimization. Since machine learning is applied so widely, many researchers have studied end-to-end techniques that combine machine learning and mathematical programming in prescriptive settings. A common approach for this is “predict-then-optimize”, where one first makes accurate predictions from data with machine learning tools, and then solves optimization problems that take these predictions as input. The criteria for improving predictions and for improving decisions are often not aligned, so a growing stream of recent work looks at more integrated, end-to-end approaches that guide decisions directly from historical data and use contextual information. To deal with the possible misalignment between the loss function of a predictive model and the objective function of the downstream optimization model, one paper defines suitable loss functions that take the downstream optimization problem into account when measuring prediction errors. It also explains how to train predictive models with these loss functions under this smart predict-then-optimize framework. Generalization bounds for the framework are then given by follow-up work. All of these papers focus on integrating predictive models that are trained with supervised learning with a downstream optimization phase. Our paper instead looks at the upstream phase of dimensionality reduction, which is a kind of unsupervised learning. Instead of making accurate predictions to inform the downstream optimization task, we want to find a low-dimensional space of features that is informative for the downstream optimization problem.

Dimensionality Reduction and Optimization. PCA has been used as the standard approach for linear dimensionality reduction when a sample covariance matrix is given. Researchers have cast the dimensionality reduction problem as minimizing the error of approximating a matrix under structural (including rank) constraints, and proposed mathematical-programming-based approaches for different variants of the problem. These studies use a mathematical programming approach like our paper does, but they consider the classic objective of minimizing reconstruction error. As we will argue later, when the low-dimensional model is fed into a stochastic programming problem afterwards, this error minimization objective is not necessarily aligned with finding good solutions with respect to the downstream objective function. To deal with this, another work proposes the directed PCA approach, which estimates the covariance matrix by balancing between the PCA objective and empirical optimization. Its aim is similar to ours, but our setting and our methodological approach are quite different. In particular, that work considers a downstream single-stage stochastic convex optimization problem with uncertain objective coefficients where the decision variables are unconstrained, while we consider a downstream two-stage stochastic program with recourse decisions that depend on the realization of uncertainty. So the low-dimensional representation governs the space of recourse decisions in the downstream problem. Also, because there are first-stage decisions in our setting, we need an approach that gives a covariance matrix that is without using the mean (i.e., invariant to the first-stage decisions) of the data. This is one of the reasons why we use distributionally-robust optimization and not Bayesian optimization as in directed PCA.

Decision Rules in Two-Stage Optimization under Uncertainty. In our setting we learn a low-dimensional representation that characterizes the uncertainty in a two-stage stochastic program with recourse. Conceptually this goal is closely linked with the literature on decision rules in multi-stage optimization with recourse. In that literature, the recourse decisions are not allowed to be optimized for the specific realizations of uncertainty, but instead they are restricted to the space of parametric functions of the realized uncertain parameters, which are called decision rules. Then the problem can be (heuristically) solved by optimizing over the space of parameters of these decision rule functions. The decision rule approach has been used in both robust optimization and stochastic programming settings. Various studies have pointed out that a careful parameterization of the primitive uncertainties of the problem is important for improving the performance of LDRs and their generalizations. Like these works, our analysis suggests that learning a suitable initial representation from data can significantly improve the performance of linear decision rules in a data-driven stochastic programming setting.

Our work is related to the literature on mathematical programming and machine learning.

Interface of Machine Learning and Optimization. In line with the prevalent application of machine learning, numerous researchers have studied end-to-end techniques that integrate machine learning and mathematical programming in prescriptive settings. A prevalent approach of this kind is “predict-then-optimize”, which involves first making accurate predictions from data using machine learning tools and then solving optimization problems that take such predictions as input [2,3]. Noting that the criteria for improving predictions and for improving decisions are often not aligned, a growing stream of recent work studies more integrated, end-to-end approaches that guide decisions directly from historical data and leverage contextual information [4,5,6]. To address the potential misalignment between the loss function of a predictive model and the objective function of the downstream optimization model, [1] define suitable loss functions that take the downstream optimization problem into account when measuring prediction errors, and elaborate on how to train predictive models with these loss functions under this smart predict-then-optimize framework. [7] further provide generalization bounds for the framework. These papers focus on integrating predictive models, trained through supervised learning, with a downstream optimization phase. Our paper, on the other hand, considers the upstream phase of dimensionality reduction, a class of unsupervised learning. Rather than making accurate predictions to inform the downstream optimization task, we aim to identify a low-dimensional space of features that is informative for the downstream optimization problem.

Dimensionality Reduction and Optimization. PCA has been adopted as the standard approach for linear dimensionality reduction given a sample covariance matrix [8]. Casting dimensionality reduction as minimizing the error in approximating a matrix subject to structural (including rank) constraints, researchers have proposed mathematical-programming-based approaches to different variants of the problem [9,10,11,12]. Although these studies take a mathematical programming approach as we do, they consider the classic objective of minimizing reconstruction error. As we argue later, when the low-dimensional model is fed into a subsequent stochastic programming problem, this objective is not necessarily aligned with identifying good solutions with respect to the downstream objective function. To address this issue, [13] propose the directed PCA approach, which estimates the covariance matrix by balancing the PCA objective and empirical optimization. While its aim is similar to ours, our setting and methodological approach differ significantly. In particular, [13] consider a downstream single-stage stochastic convex optimization problem with uncertain objective coefficients and unconstrained decision variables, whereas we consider a downstream two-stage stochastic program with recourse decisions that depend on the realization of uncertainty. The low-dimensional representation therefore governs the space of recourse decisions in the downstream problem. Further, the presence of first-stage decisions in our setting requires an approach that yields a covariance matrix that is without using the mean (i.e., invariant to the first-stage decisions) of the data. This is one of our motivations for using distributionally-robust optimization rather than Bayesian optimization as in [13].

Decision Rules in Two-Stage Optimization under Uncertainty. Our setting concerns learning a low-dimensional representation that characterizes the uncertainty in a two-stage stochastic program with recourse. Conceptually, this objective is closely linked to the literature on decision rules in multi-stage optimization with recourse. There, instead of allowing recourse decisions to be optimized for specific realizations of uncertainty, they are confined to a space of parametric functions of the realized uncertain parameters, known as decision rules. The problem can then be (heuristically) solved by optimizing over the parameters of these decision rule functions. The decision rule approach has been adopted in both robust optimization and stochastic programming settings [14,15,16,17,18,19]. Various studies have pointed out the importance of carefully parameterizing the primitive uncertainties of the problem to enhance the performance of LDRs and their generalizations [20,21,22]. Similarly, our analysis suggests that learning an appropriate initial representation from data can significantly improve the performance of linear decision rules in a data-driven stochastic programming setting.
